newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia broke UN arms ban - Jansa.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia broke UN arms ban - Jansa.

text.p: Former jailed dissident Janez Jansa, who earned hero status during Slovenia's independence war as defence minister, said his country, Croatia and Bosnia defied a U.N. arms embargo to buy weapons illegally.
Jansa, Slovenian defence minister from 1990 until he was sacked in March 1994, said the ex-Yugoslav republics had no choice but to circumvent the arms ban to fight for statehood.
"Everybody knew Slovenia had to buy weapons illegally before the war, during the war and during the embargo, otherwise this would still bgoslavia," he told Reuters in an interview at the weekend.
The U.N. Security Council in June lifted an arms ban on the republics of former Yugoslavia, in force since September 1991.

"Before my replacement, we made complete reports of these (arms) transactions even for Croatia and Bosnia. It is written down," said Jansa, jailed by communist Yugoslav authorities in 1988 for calling for multi-party democracy in Slovenia, Yugoslavia's richest and most ethnically-homogeneous republic.
He said the decisions to buy and supply arms were taken by Slovenia's National Defence Council, headed by President Milan Kucan.
Jansa has made similar comments in the past, which put him on a collision course with Kucan while he was still defence minister, and which indirectly led to his downfall.
Now, he said, with the embargo lifted, there would be no harm for the government of Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek to make public the documents on the arms purchases.

"It is not so important after the lifting of the embargo. But before it was not sensib He said Kucan had been the first point of contact by Croatia and Bosnia. "It was our president who was first asked, and after that, things started to move."
Jansa now heads the Social Democratic Party and is bidding for power in general elections scheduled for November 10.

He won nationwide acclaim and hero status for organising ich outmanoeuvred the Yugoslav federal army in Slovenia's 10-day independence war in June 1991. Jansa dismisses suggestions that he tarnished his reputation by attacking Kucan, who remains enormously popular in Slovenia.

He pointed to results of local elections last year in which the Social Democrats secured 14 percent of the vote. Recent polls show his party with the second biggest backing of around nine percent, behind Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats on 16 percent.
Jansa hopes to form a coalition with the rightist People's Party and conservative Christian Democrats in a partnership known as "the Slovenian Spring".
A firm backer of Slovenian membership of NATO and the European Union, Jansa said Drnovsek had avoided taking the hard economic decisions needed to prepare for EU entry.

He proposes a radical reform of the pensions systems to rein in public spending and said support had to be directed to small and medium-sized businesses instead of propping up large enterprises. Wholesale privatisation of the banking sector was also crucial to boost the Slovenian economy, he added.

While many of his economic ideas may be considered firmly on the right, Jansa said 60 percent of Social Democrat members were workers and the party would fight for social justice in a free market economy.
